Threat.value: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
Irritable behavior, angry outbursts, or acting aggressively

Memory.value: I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns
My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.
When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once

Negative Appraisals.value: People are not what they seem

vignette: Six months ago, Maya was navigating the turnstiles of the downtown transit hub, her violin case resting against her hip, on her way to an afternoon recording session. The air had been dry, carrying the familiar blend of roasted coffee and polished concrete. Then the blast ripped through the ticketing concourse. The ceiling groaned, glass shredded the atmosphere, and a thick, chemical smoke rolled over her. She tasted copper and burnt wiring, the same metallic grit that coated her tongue as she pressed herself into the narrow gap behind a concrete pillar, listening to the synchronized rush of sirens and panicked footsteps. When the dust finally settled, she walked out into the street with her hands trembling, the ordinary city around her suddenly rendered alien. The memories never softened at the edges. They arrived with startling clarity, every fractured tile, every flickering departure board, every face caught mid-scream preserved in sharp relief. Maya found that the past did not linger; it overwrote the present. On a Tuesday afternoon, while sitting in the corner of a community rehearsal studio, a delivery van’s backfire echoed through the open window. The sound collapsed the room. She was back against the pillar, the air suddenly thick with the same choking smoke, the taste of burnt copper flooding her mouth. She dropped her rosin, scrambling backward until her spine hit the wall, her breath coming in short, sharp pulls. The memories did not ask for permission. They arrived as total sensory invasions, pulling her out of the present and dropping her into the exact moment the space had shattered. In the weeks that followed, the memories arrived alongside her daily routines. She sat at her drafting table to sketch out a composition for a local chamber ensemble, but her eyes would slide past the staff lines. The notation blurred into meaningless geometry, and her mind refused to hold the sequence in place. She caught herself tracing the same measure over and over, her attention fracturing every time a colleague’s voice rose or a door slammed down the hall. When her ensemble leader called to check her progress, a sudden heat flooded her chest. She snapped at him, her words sharp and unrecognizable, before hanging up and staring at her hands. The irritability came first, a sudden, surging force that left her isolated and unable to explain herself. She stopped returning messages from former bandmates. People who had shared stages with her for years now felt like strangers wearing careful masks, their expressions impossible to read. Maya found herself leaving group rehearsals early, citing a heavy schedule, but the reality was quieter and heavier. She could not stand the feeling of being surrounded by bodies who might shift from familiar to threatening without warning. The city, once a network of possibilities, now felt like a confined space with no clear exits. She stayed in her apartment most days, drawing the blinds, telling herself it was safer. Her partner, David, would ask her to go out for dinner, to walk through the park, to remember who she used to be. She would shake her head, her chest tightening. There was no future to look toward, only the long, quiet stretch of days where she waited for the next time the ground would give way. It was the stillness in her living room that finally broke her. She had stopped composing for months. Her instruments sat in the corner, gathering dust, and the space around her felt like it belonged to no one, not even her. She sat on the floor, staring at her phone, knowing she could not keep tracing the same measure of her life on loop. She had come to believe that the person she was before that afternoon in the station was gone, and she had no idea how to meet the days ahead. When she finally called the clinic, her hands were cold. She did not want to be afraid anymore. She did not want to wake up tasting smoke. She just wanted to know if she could ever feel like she belonged anywhere again.
